metadata.title: PISA 2018 Results (Volume III): What School Life Means for Students’ Lives

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA 2018 volume reports results based on the PISA international assessment design, which uses complex sampling of students within schools and schools within education systems. The report notes that when principals’ responses are presented, they are weighted so that they are proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, indicating the use of sampling/coverage weights for school-level reporting. For student-level indicators, the publication relies on the OECD PISA database and standard PISA estimation procedures; however, the provided excerpt does not specify the exact student weight variable names or replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because this is a framework/report-style extraction rather than an ML re-analysis, the manuscript excerpt does not document the analyst-facing weight variable names; users should consult the PISA 2018 Technical Report for the exact weighting and variance estimation specifications.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable here because the excerpted content is an OECD PISA results volume describing reported indicators (e.g., bullying prevalence, life satisfaction, growth mindset) and does not provide an explicit PV-based achievement modeling pipeline. The excerpt also does not document a specific missing-data handling strategy for any PV-based estimation (e.g., PV imputation/combining rules or missing questionnaire item treatment). This is therefore a reporting/coverage gap in the provided text rather than evidence that missingness was absent.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt describes PISA 2018 coverage of 15-year-olds (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) enrolled in school and having completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of institution type. It also states that the volume features data on 79 countries and economies and that B-S-J-Z (China) refers to the four participating provinces/municipalities (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang). No explicit analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., specific grade bands, CBA modules, or exclusion rules beyond general PISA exclusions) are provided in the excerpt; therefore, the filtering criteria cannot be specified beyond the standard PISA target population definition.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2018 Results (Volume III) report synthesises cross-national evidence on school climate and students’ well-being for the PISA target population of 15-year-olds. It reports indicators such as bullying exposure and anti-bullying attitudes, disciplinary climate in language-of-instruction lessons, student co-operation/competition, teacher support and enthusiasm, student truancy and lateness, and well-being measures including life satisfaction, positive/negative feelings, self-efficacy, fear of failure, and growth mindset. The report uses PISA’s international assessment framework and standardised questionnaires administered to students, principals, and parents, and it presents results as OECD averages and cross-system comparisons across 79 education systems/economies. The excerpted material includes regression-based associations (e.g., accounting for ESCS, gender, and reading performance) and provides significance conventions, but it does not document an ML prediction pipeline or the exact PV/missing-data handling steps in the provided text. Policy implications emphasise that school climate and supportive teaching practices are linked to reading outcomes and students’ well-being, and that equity-focused improvements are needed where bullying, lateness, and low well-being are more prevalent.
